report.answer_text:
On October 22, 2025, Google reported that its Willow quantum chip ran an algorithm called Quantum Echoes in about two hours. Google estimated that the best known classical method would take 13,000 times as long on one of the world’s fastest supercomputers. The results were published in *Nature*. (research.google)
Google called it the first verifiable quantum advantage: a comparably capable quantum computer could repeat the calculation and check the result. The speedup was for one specific task—measuring how a disturbance spreads through a quantum system—not a claim that Willow is faster than supercomputers at everything. Google also reported a separate proof-of-concept experiment using the technique to study molecular structure. (blog.google)

quotes.text: In our latest Nature publication, we introduce a new quantum computational task measuring Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs).

pages.quote_reason: The quote says a Nature publication introduces a quantum task measuring OTOCs, which supports publication in Nature, but it does not name Google or the Quantum Echoes experiment.
pages.page_reason: The page states that 'In our latest Nature publication' they introduce OTOC work and that 'Observation of constructive interference at the edge of quantum ergodicity', featured on the cover of Nature, introduces the Quantum Echoes algorithm, so the claim is supported.

claims.sentence: Google also reported a separate proof-of-concept experiment using the technique to study molecular structure. (blog.google)
claims.claim: Google also reported a separate proof-of-concept experiment using the Quantum Echoes technique to study molecular structure.
claims.label: supported

pages.label: supported

quotes.text: In a separate, proof-of-principle experiment Quantum computation of molecular geometry via many-body nuclear spin echoes (to be posted on arXiv later today), we showed how our new technique — a “molecular ruler” — can measure longer distances than today’s methods, using data from Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) to gain more information about chemical structure.

In a proof-of-principle experiment in partnership with The University of California, Berkeley, we ran the Quantum Echoes algorithm on our Willow chip to study two molecules, one with 15 atoms and another with 28 atoms, to verify this approach.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes state a separate proof-of-principle experiment that ran the Quantum Echoes algorithm on Google's Willow chip to study molecular geometry and structure, which covers everything the claim says.
pages.page_reason: The page describes a separate proof-of-principle experiment (the 'molecular ruler' paper on molecular geometry via nuclear spin echoes), and a later section says the Quantum Echoes algorithm was run on Willow to study molecular structure in a proof-of-principle experiment, which combines to support the claim.
